name: State Channel
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Take It Off-Chain and Settle Later: The State Channel
lesson.summary: A state channel lets a small group of participants lock funds or data on a blockchain, then exchange an unlimited number of signed updates directly with each other off-chain, only returning to the base chain to open and finally close the channel.
lesson.body:
Layer 2 solutions, covered in the previous chapter, are systems built on top of a base blockchain that move most transaction activity off that chain while relying on it for final settlement. A state channel is one of the earliest and most concrete implementations of that idea. It works by having a small group of participants, often just two, submit a single on-chain transaction that locks funds or an initial agreed state into a shared arrangement, typically a multi-signature contract that requires agreement from the participants to release, opening the channel.

Once the channel is open, the real efficiency shows up. Participants exchange signed messages directly with each other, off-chain, and each new message updates the agreed state, for example a running balance between the two parties, superseding whatever the previous message said. None of these intermediate updates touch the blockchain at all. They are not limited by block time, by the base chain's throughput, or by transaction fees, since no other node in the network is involved in exchanging them, and their speed depends only on the network latency directly between the participants themselves, exactly the network latency concept covered much earlier in this book.

Closing the channel is what finally brings the interaction back on-chain. Either participant can submit the latest, most recent signed state to the blockchain, which settles the true final outcome, releasing the locked funds according to that final balance. Because a participant could try to cheat by submitting an old, outdated state that favored them more than the true latest state does, most state channel designs include a challenge period after a closing transaction is submitted, during which the other party can present a newer signed state to override it. This is why usable state channel implementations generally require participants to remain able to monitor the chain during that challenge window, at least periodically, rather than being able to walk away and check back only much later.

The clearest real world example is Bitcoin's Lightning Network, a payment channel network, essentially a specialized state channel design focused purely on balance updates, that allows two users to route a payment across a network of already open channels, with settlement measured in milliseconds and fees a small fraction of what an equivalent on-chain Bitcoin transaction costs. This is exactly the kind of throughput and latency improvement, both concepts covered earlier, that off-chain designs are built to deliver.

The trade off is that state channels work best for participants who transact with each other repeatedly over time and already have, or are willing to set up, a channel between them. They do not help with a genuinely one off payment to a stranger unless some existing path of open channels happens to connect the two parties, and locking funds into a channel ties up that capital until the channel eventually closes, which is the real cost behind the channel's otherwise near limitless off-chain speed.
